Overview
Periprosthetic fractures around total knee arthroplasty (TKA) implants are uncommon. They
can involve the distal femur, proximal tibia, or patella.
Complications of TKA, including periprosthetic fractures, cost an estimated $2.7 billion
annually in the United States, and this number is expected to rise as the incidence of TKA
increases.1
Periprosthetic femur fractures after TKA are associated with a higher morbidity and mortality
(27% 1-year mortality rate) than primary TKA or distal femur fractures without TKA.2 Therefore,
proper preventative strategies, implant selection, and treatment plans are important.
Periprosthetic fractures of the femur, tibia, and patella are discussed in this lesson. Most of
this lesson focuses on postoperative periprosthetic fractures; however, information on
intraoperative fractures is included in the appropriate sections (Resource 1).
Epidemiology
The incidence of periprosthetic fractures of the distal femur after TKA ranges from 0.3% to
2.5%. These fractures occur more commonly in the distal femur than in the tibia and patella.3
The incidence after revision TKA is higher (28%).3
The incidence of periprosthetic tibia fracture after primary TKA ranges from 0.4% to 1.7%, and
the incidence of periprosthetic tibia fracture after revision TKA is 0.9%.3

Epidemiology
Periprosthetic fractures of the distal femur are the most common complication
associated with TKA, with a reported incidence ranging from 0.3% to 2.5% after primary
TKA4 and as high as 28% after revision TKA.5 Periprosthetic tibia fractures occur in 0.4%
to 1.7% of patients after primary TKA and in 0.9% of patients after revision TKA.6 Females
are more commonly affected than males, with the mean age ranging from 64 to 74
years.1 Therefore, a comprehensive assessment of comorbidities and optimization
before surgical management is essential, if possible, to minimize complications.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
A medial parapatellar arthrotomy is the most commonly used approach for primary and
revision TKA. The revision surgeon must be aware of extensile measures (quadriceps
snip, quadriceps turndown, or tibial tubercle osteotomy) that may be required if
exposure is difficult. The medial and lateral collateral ligaments may be involved in
fracture fragments, more commonly on the femoral side, and must be carefully studied
in planning revision and fixation options.
Popliteal artery injury is a rare but potentially devastating injury that occurs in
approximately 0.05% of patients. Revision surgery and peripheral vascular disease are
two of the risk factors for popliteal artery injury that should be considered in patients
with a periprosthetic fracture.7

Trauma/falls
High-energy trauma in younger patients
Removal or insertion of components during revision surgery

The most common mechanism of postoperative periprosthetic fractures is trauma,
particularly falls. Low-energy falls are a common etiology in the elderly population,

population. Intraoperative fractures often result from risk factors, such as osteoporosis,
poor bone quality, and osteolysis. Intraoperative fractures generally occur during
removal or impaction of components, especially in patients who have undergone prior
revision, patients with osteolysis, and patients with poor bone quality.8
Risk Factors
Common risk factors include advanced age, rheumatoid or inflammatory arthropathy,
neurologic disorders, chronic steroid therapy, osteopenia, and osteoporosis.3
Diabetes mellitus may affect stability and balance, which may predispose patients to recurrent
falls.9
Other risk factors include component malalignment, particularly in the tibia; component
removal during revision; and tibial tubercle osteotomy.3
Anterior femoral notching has been debated as a risk factor.3,8
Component loosening and osteolysis with bone loss is an important risk factor and may
substantially affect revision options.3

Risk Factors
Revision TKA is a major risk factor for intraoperative and postoperative fracture, and the
incidence ranges from 1.7% to 2.5%.10,11 In particular, patients with a nonunion are five
times more likely to sustain a postoperative periprosthetic fracture.11 Preexisting
infection and revision procedures requiring component removal also are important risk
factors to consider.3
Anterior femoral notching is a controversial risk factor. A cadaver model study found
that torsional strength had a 31% decrease to failure after notching;12 however, later
studies have shown no association between notching and subsequent supracondylar
fractures.13-15 The general consensus in the literature is that notching is not associated
with supracondylar fractures.

Injury Classification
The UCS has become increasingly used in the periprosthetic literature and has been
adapted by the AO Foundation as the primary classification system for periprosthetic
fractures22-24 (Table 2). The UCS describes six types of fractures, from A to F; each type
describes a specific fracture pattern and involvement of the prosthetic component. This
classification system can be applied to any joint with a prosthesis and uses the principles
of periprosthetic fracture management in a universal and consistent manner. UCS type B
fractures involving the supracondylar distal femur are the most common TKA fracture
subtype, occurring 73% of the time.25,26
Although the UCS is becoming more popular, tibial fractures are commonly described
using the Felix classification system16 (Figure 1). Ultimately, the principles of
management, regardless of the classification system, are similar.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A complete medical history is required because this patient population often has
comorbidities.
Preinjury concerns with knee arthroplasty should be elicited.
Prior surgical records for knee arthroplasty should be obtained.

Patient History
A complete patient history, including all comorbidities and medications, should be
obtained. Considerable medical comorbidities should be appropriately managed before
surgical treatment.27 A multidisciplinary approach has been shown to decrease
morbidity and mortality rates in patients with a periprosthetic fracture.28 Any preinjury

drainage/sinus tract postoperatively, should be explored because they may represent
preexisting conditions, such as aseptic loosening or infection. If infection is suspected,
infection markers, such as C-reactive protein level or erythrocyte sedimentation rate,
should be obtained. Aspiration also should be considered in patients in whom infection
is suspected. Surgical details and implant records pertaining to the underlying TKA
implant should be obtained.
Physical Examination
A detailed physical examination is necessary, especially in a polytrauma patient in whom
Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol may be required.
Careful examination of the knee should be performed, with assessment of prior incisions and
any abnormalities.
A detailed neurologic examination is required.

Physical Examination
A detailed physical examination should be performed. In a polytrauma patient,
Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol should be followed. Involvement of medical and
anesthesia personnel is necessary for patients with multiple medical concerns. Incisional
locations and appearance and any swelling, erythema, sinus tracts, or other signs of
infection should be noted. Range of motion and stability testing likely will be difficult
because of pain and the underlying fracture. Surgeons must determine the status of the
extensor mechanism, if possible. A comprehensive assessment of other associated
injuries from a trauma mechanism of injury should be performed.
Neurovascular Examination
Neurologic and vascular injuries are rare but should be part of the complete physical
examination.

Neurovascular Examination
A detailed neurologic and vascular examination of the lower extremity should be
performed. Because peripheral vascular disease is common in older populations,
documentation of absent or decreased pulses via Doppler should be performed.
Although vascular injuries are uncommon, any suspicion of a vascular injury should be
promptly investigated.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs, including AP and lateral views
CT scans
Bone scans
Radiography
At least two views (AP and lateral) are necessary to identify the type and extent of the fracture.
Radiographs should be assessed for signs of component or cement loosening.3
Prior radiographs should be obtained for comparison.
Radiographs of ipsilateral hip and femur

Radiography
Radiographs should be examined for signs of component loosening and osteolysis,
implant wear, and malpositioning.27 Radiographs of the ipsilateral hip and femur should
be obtained so that revision stem length, if applicable, can be appropriately templated
and selected. In addition, if an ipsilateral hip replacement is present, the distance
between the existing hip implant and the planned knee revision component should be
determined. If the stems are in close proximity, a stress riser–inducing scenario exists,
which can be prevented with the use of an osteosynthesis plate or a strut allograft.29

Computed Tomography
CT scans may serve as an additional imaging study to document fracture pattern and
component loosening. Distal femur fracture lines often are distorted with metal artifact.
Bone Scintigraphy
A bone scan may help identify a fracture if plain radiographs are not diagnostic, such as in
patients with a stress fracture.3
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most periprosthetic fractures of the femur are managed via surgical fixation.
Nonsurgical management may be considered for some UCS type A fractures of the femur or
tibia if they are nondisplaced and stable.
Nonsurgical management of nondisplaced fractures should be considered in patients who are
poor surgical candidates. Close follow-up should be considered in patients treated
nonsurgically because reduction may be difficult to maintain.3
Conversion to surgical management may be considered in patients in whom nonsurgical
treatment fails.8
Tibial fractures, if nondisplaced, stable, and not associated with component loosening, may be
managed via casting or bracing techniques and protected–weight bearing.3,30
Indications
Nonsurgical management of distal femur fractures may be considered in elderly patients,
patients with low baseline mobility, and patients with considerable comorbidities that pose an
unacceptably high risk for surgical management.8
Patient selection is critical because nonsurgical management is associated with a higher risk of
nonunion and malunion compared with surgical fixation, with prolonged periods of
immobilization.31
Nondisplaced proximal tibia fractures without component loosening or patients who are poor
surgical candidates20

Relative contraindications to nonsurgical treatment include patients who are unable to

Techniques/Procedures
Long leg cast or brace immobilization should be used. Cast immobilization may be required in
patients who cannot tolerate a brace.
A period of non–weight bearing is required until radiographic union.
Skin care with cast and brace immobilization is critical, particularly in low-mobility, elderly
patients.
Frequent radiographs should be obtained until union is achieved.
Transition to surgical management may be required if nonsurgical management fails.
Surgical Management
Most periprosthetic fractures that occur around a TKA implant, especially the distal femur,
should be managed surgically.3
Surgical management typically allows for early range of motion, avoids prolonged
immobilization, and reduces the risk of fracture displacement.3

Surgical Management
Several surgical treatment options are available to manage these injuries, including open
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), intramedullary nailing (IMN), and revision
arthroplasty. Treatment option selection is guided by implant stability, bone stock, and
overall patient health and functional demands. The principles of management align with
the UCS and also are described in other classification systems. Regardless of the
classification system used, the general principles of surgical management are similar.

Most periprosthetic fractures involving the femur require surgical fixation. Select nondisplaced
tibial fractures may be managed nonsurgically.
Surgical management generally is indicated for displaced fractures and those with loose
components.
Keys to surgical fixation include restoration of anatomic alignment with adequate fixation,
restoration of the joint line and patellofemoral mechanics, revision of unstable arthroplasty
components, and restoration of ligamentous stability via fracture fixation or revision
arthroplasty.3
Contraindications
Patients unsuitable for surgical treatment
Polytrauma patients may require medical stabilization or other treatment options before
management of periprosthetic injuries.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning for the management of periprosthetic fractures of the tibia and femur is
critical.
Radiographs of the entire femur and tibia should be obtained.
All implant records and details of existing arthroplasty components should be obtained.
Preexisting bone loss and any prior radiographs should be studied.
Symptoms suggestive of periprosthetic infection should be appropriately assessed.
The status of the medial and lateral collateral ligaments should be considered in the surgical
plan.


surgeon must be prepared with several treatment options; fixation, revision
arthroplasty, and distal femur replacement are among the options, depending on the
scenario. An ipsilateral total hip implant may preclude the use of certain stem lengths or

All implant records should be obtained before surgical fixation. Confirming whether the

aspiration if possible.8
Restoration of coronal stability is important. Fragments attached to the medial collateral
ligament or the lateral collateral ligament should be secured via fixation or revision
options, if possible. If this is not possible, a constrained, hinged, or distal femur
replacement should be considered.

Medial parapatellar arthrotomy is the preferred approach for retrograde IMN or revision
arthroplasty.

Distal Femur Fractures
In patients with a supracondylar fracture proximal to the femoral component, ORIF with
the use of a fixed-angle device, such as locking or nonlocking plates, a blade plate, or a
condylar screw plate or a retrograde IMN, allows for fracture fixation while preserving
the underlying TKA implant.3,8 However, time to union may be prolonged and weight
bearing may not be possible for several months.34 Minimally invasive techniques with
the use of modern plates have become commonly used, and this method may be
associated with a lower nonunion rate.35
Debate exists regarding the retrograde IMN versus plating techniques for supracondylar
fractures. Retrograde nailing is only possible in certain types of femoral implants, which
underscores the importance of obtaining implant records before management. Several
studies comparing locked plating versus retrograde nails have reported varied results. In
a study of 85 patients, Meneghini et al36 found only one nonunion in the IMN group and
12 nonunions in the plating group. Conversely, in a large systemic review of over 719
fractures, Ristevski et al37 reported a substantial advantage to locked plating. The
authors proposed that difficulty with starting point location in the retrograde IMN group
led to inferior outcomes. In addition, fewer options were available distally for fixation
and maintenance of reduction. Kiluçoğlu et al38 reported no difference between the two
methods. A recent meta-analysis did not find a difference in time to union or nonunion
rate.39 Therefore, no clear answer exists with regard to which method is superior;
however, if retrograde IMN nailing is undertaken, great care should be exercised to
ensure a correct starting point and that adequate distal fixation is attained.8
If a loose component is encountered, revision arthroplasty with the use of a stemmed
component, with or without plate fixation as an adjunct, is an option, given that
supportive bone stock is present.3 Ligamentous laxity in this scenario may be managed
via a constrained revision system. Structural allograft, augments, or metaphyseal cones
or sleeves can be used to manage bone loss.3 A DFR component may be considered if

Risk Factors
Osteonecrosis has been identified as an important risk factor for patellar periprosthetic
fracture. After the medial parapatellar approach and lateral meniscectomy, which occurs
during standard exposure for TKA, the only remaining extraosseous vessel is the
superior genicular artery. Lateral retinacular release may affect this remaining supply,
resulting in an increased risk for necrosis and subsequent periprosthetic fracture.59,60
Patellar thickness also is a risk for fracture. Although variable, patellar thickness of less
than 13 mm is thought to be associated with increased risk. A study reported that, even
if the original thickness is re-created with the use of a correct prosthesis, the patella only
retains 75% of its strength.61
Certain implant designs have been associated with increased risk of periprosthetic
fracture. Metal-backed patella components are subject to early loosening and fracture,
which is thought to result from increased component stiffness.59,62 In addition, a large
central peg58 and inset designs also are associated with increased risk of fracture.

Injuries with extensor mechanism disruption are managed surgically via ORIF, if amenable.3

Surgical Management
The surgical management of these injuries depends on the quality of the extensor
mechanism and the underlying bone. A medial parapatellar approach is adequate for
exposure and fixation. If bone stock is adequate, the patella is fixed via ORIF, often with
the use of tension band wiring (Figure 10). If the underlying bone stock is poor, partial
patellectomy with suture repair through bone tunnels may be attempted. Total
patellectomy with soft-tissue allograft reconstruction of the extensor mechanism can be
performed if no salvageable bone remains. Loose patella components typically are
removed.58 Tubularization of the extensor mechanism or bone grafting in a synovial
pouch may be considered in patients with extremely poor bone stock or considerable
comminution.3 Fixation or repair should be protected via brace or cast immobilization,
with slow restoration of range of motion after bony union is achieved.
Malaligned tibial and femoral components should be inspected before revision, or the
surgeon should be prepared for revision if intraoperative inspection reveals
malalignment. Malalignment contributes to patellar fractures and should be addressed
at the time of revision.
